Paper: Ho and Salimans (2022), [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598).
Classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens conditioning at sampling time by combining conditional and unconditional predictions from a jointly trained diffusion model.
It provides an adjustable fidelity–diversity trade-off without a separate classifier's gradients.

## Problem

A conditional generative model represents a distribution of possible outputs for a condition $c$, such as an image class.
Ordinary conditional sampling need not provide the desired balance between variety and strong agreement with that condition.
The paper seeks a sampling-time control over this balance for diffusion models. [Paper, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=2).

## Previous attempts

In discrete models, temperature sampling rescales logits before softmax, $p_i\propto\exp(l_i/T)$.
Latent truncation changes the distribution of starting codes in certain generative models.
Neither construction directly supplies the noisy-state conditioning direction used by classifier guidance.
The CFG paper discusses these approaches as motivation for controlling diffusion sampling. [Paper, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=2).

Classifier guidance uses a classifier adapted to noisy inputs and adds its conditional log-probability gradient to the diffusion score.
Training and maintaining this additional classifier introduces a separate modelling requirement.
It does not inherently mean adversarial training, nor does the method require that the classifier's parameters always be initialised from scratch. [Paper, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=4).

## Proposed solution

During training, randomly replace the designated condition with a null condition for some examples.
The noisy sample and noise-level information remain present.
The same denoiser therefore learns both $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c)$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,\varnothing)$. [Paper, Algorithm 1 and §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=4).

At each sampling step, evaluate both versions and combine them:

$$
  \tilde\epsilon=(1+w)\epsilon_{\mathrm{cond}}
  -w\epsilon_{\mathrm{uncond}}.
$$

The paper's convention uses $w=0$ for ordinary conditional sampling and $w>0$ for extrapolation beyond it.
A common equivalent convention writes

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \tilde\epsilon={}&\epsilon_{\mathrm{uncond}}\\
  &+\gamma(\epsilon_{\mathrm{cond}}-\epsilon_{\mathrm{uncond}}),
  \end{aligned}
$$

where $\gamma=1+w$.
Under the second convention, $\gamma=1$ means ordinary conditional prediction and $\gamma=0$ means unconditional prediction.
Reporting a guidance scale without its formula leaves this convention ambiguous. [Paper, Eq. (6) and Algorithm 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=5).

The combination enters the sampler in place of the ordinary denoising prediction.
It is not simply a final subtraction of two generated images.

## Why the difference carries conditioning information

At a fixed noise level, define exact conditional and unconditional scores by

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  s_c(x)&=\nabla_x\log p_t(x\mid c),\\
  s_u(x)&=\nabla_x\log p_t(x).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Bayes' rule gives

$$
  s_c(x)-s_u(x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(c\mid x).
$$

Thus, with exact scores, their difference acts like a noisy-input classifier gradient.
Noise predictions and scores are related by the same noise-level scaling, so the linear CFG combination can be expressed in either parameterisation. [Paper, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=5).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: Bayes' rule and the idealised density tilt"}

Take the logarithm of Bayes' rule:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \log p_t(x\mid c)
  & =\log p_t(c\mid x)\\
  &\quad+\log p_t(x)-\log p(c).
  \end{aligned}
$$

The final term is constant with respect to $x$, so differentiation yields the score-difference identity.
For exact scores, the guided field is

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  s_g&=(1+w)s_c-ws_u\\
  &=\nabla_x\log\left[
  p_t(x\mid c)^{1+w}p_t(x)^{-w}\right].
  \end{aligned}
$$

If the expression can be normalised, this describes a tilted density at that fixed time.
It does not by itself prove that a finite-step guided reverse sampler produces a corresponding simple density tilt at the final endpoint.
Furthermore, learned score fields need not be exact gradients of any scalar density, a qualification the paper explicitly discusses.

:::

## Evidence

The experiments use class-conditional ImageNet generation and study how guidance strength changes sample metrics and diversity.
They show that the proposed combination can provide a trade-off similar to classifier guidance without training a separate classifier. [Paper, §4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12598#page=5).
These experiments establish the method for the tested class-conditioned diffusion models, rather than a universal best scale for every condition or domain.

## Limitations

The basic method requires two denoiser evaluations per sampling step, even when implementations batch them together.
Stronger guidance can reduce diversity, and increasing the scale does not guarantee monotonic improvement in every quality measure.
Conditioning dropout must prepare the model for its null-condition query; dropping arbitrary inputs from an otherwise conditional model is not equivalent training.
